newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich returns to political turmoil on ethics.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich returns to political turmoil on ethics.

text.p: House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich returned to Washington on Thursday, heading into a political maelstrom whirling around the last stage of an investigation into ethics charges against him.

Gingrich flew in from his home state of Georgia following a week of turmoil and political recriminations, as a special counsel worked against a midnight deadline to provide a badly torn House ethics committee his report on his year-long investigation.
Asked about the investigation as he arrived at the Capitol, Gingrich said: "We're going to do whatever we're asked to do and we're going to try to be helpful."

But Democrats continued to rail against a midnight Tuesday deadline for a final House vote on the punishment to be meted out to Gingrich for his admitted ethics violations. He is widely expected to be given a reprimand, which would not force him to step down.

"We are outraged, we are frustrated ... at a process that has been so truncated and so manipulated," Democratic Caucus chairman Vic Fazio told reporters. "It's going to leave a scar on the institution. The Republicans have put before anything else the preservation of the power of the speaker."
Gingrich, however, appeared upbeat about the upcoming congressional session, saying, "I think we're going to have a very productive year."

Gingrich admitted "with great sadness" on Dec. 21 that he had provided to investigators "in my name and over my signature, inaccurate, incomplete and unreliable statements." He said he had not intended to mislead the committee.

He also acknowledged he had failed to seek legal advice on whether his use of tax-exempt charitable funds for a college course he taught would violate tax laws. The subcommittee did not take a position on whether the law had been broken.

Cole was closeted in a room in a House office building on Thursday working on his report. The Republican committee chairwoman, Nancy Johnson of Connecticut, has said it will not be made public immediately, although it was due to be delivered to the committee by day's end on Thursday.
